questions.title: What gives the Fifth Circuit appellate jurisdiction over the government’s appeal from a dismissal of an indictment?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed the indictment pretrial, and the government appealed. I thought the government’s ability to appeal in criminal cases is limited. Under what statute (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 3731?) and doctrinal framework does the Fifth Circuit have jurisdiction here, and why isn’t double jeopardy a bar when the case was dismissed before trial?

questions.title: Why is the sufficiency of an indictment reviewed de novo, and what does ‘taking the allegations as true’ actually mean?
questions.question_body: The panel says it reviews the sufficiency of an indictment de novo and must accept the indictment’s allegations as true. Is this because sufficiency is a pure question of law under Rule 12(b)? Does this mean the court cannot consider exhibits or competing factual inferences (e.g., defendants’ tweets or trading records) at this stage, even if they might show the statements weren’t misleading?

questions.title: How is ‘standing’ relevant, if at all, in a federal criminal fraud prosecution like this one?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly refers to victims (the social-media followers) but does not analyze Article III standing as in civil cases. In criminal prosecutions, is ‘standing’ simply not a requirement the court must address, with subject-matter jurisdiction grounded in the federal criminal statute? If so, what replaces the standing inquiry—just the statutory elements (e.g., that someone’s money or property was the object of the fraud)?

questions.title: Why did the court import mail/wire fraud doctrines into 18 U.S.C. § 1348 securities fraud?
questions.question_body: The panel relies on Greenlaw to treat § 1348 as borrowing ‘key concepts’ from mail and wire fraud. What is the interpretive basis for that borrowing (textual similarities, legislative history, or consistent circuit practice)? Are there any limits—i.e., doctrines that apply in mail/wire fraud but not in § 1348—given the different statutory language and context?

questions.title: Does § 1348(1) itself require that ‘obtaining money or property’ be an object of the scheme, or is that requirement coming from Ciminelli/Kousisis via analogy?
questions.question_body: Section 1348 has two clauses: (1) a scheme to defraud any person in connection with a security, and (2) a scheme to obtain money or property by false pretenses in connection with the purchase or sale of a security. The opinion repeatedly emphasizes that ‘obtaining money or property’ must be an object of the fraud. Is the court reading that requirement into clause (1) as well, or is it saying the indictment satisfies clause (2)? How do Ciminelli and Kousisis constrain clause (1), if at all?

questions.title: What exactly distinguishes the prohibited ‘right-to-control’ theory from the permitted ‘fraudulent-inducement’ theory?
questions.question_body: The panel says Ciminelli forecloses convictions based on depriving a victim of ‘valuable economic information’ alone, but Kousisis allows ‘fraudulent inducement’—tricking a victim into handing over money or property. In practice, how do courts police the line so the government cannot simply re-label right-to-control cases as ‘inducement’? What features of this indictment (inducing followers to buy securities) make it materially different from right-to-control?

questions.title: How does the court reconcile its earlier ‘intent to cause some harm’ requirement with Kousisis’s statement that net economic loss isn’t required?
questions.question_body: The opinion quotes Fifth Circuit law that intent to defraud includes intent to deceive and to cause some harm, but then relies on Kousisis that a defendant need not seek to make the victim worse off financially. Do courts now treat the ‘harm’ prong as satisfied when the object is to obtain the victim’s money or property by deceit, even if the victim receives equivalent value?

questions.title: Why doesn’t receiving market-value securities defeat the ‘scheme to defraud’ element?
questions.question_body: Defendants argued followers weren’t injured because they received market-value securities. The court says fraud is complete upon deceptive inducement to part with money or property. What is the doctrinal basis for treating the induced transfer (rather than net loss) as the injury, and how does this avoid collapsing into a broad right-to-control theory?

questions.title: What is the materiality standard under § 1348, and how do misstatements about one’s trading positions qualify?
questions.question_body: The court says a scheme to defraud requires a material misrepresentation. Is ‘materiality’ under § 1348 the same as in mail/wire fraud (capable of influencing a reasonable person) or the securities-law standard from Basic/Matrixx? Why are false statements about holding/selling a stock deemed material in this criminal context?

questions.title: Does criminal § 1348 require proof of reliance or loss causation like private Rule 10b-5 actions?
questions.question_body: The opinion does not mention reliance or loss causation. In criminal securities fraud under § 1348, is the government required to show that a victim relied on the misstatement or that the misstatement caused a pecuniary loss, or are those civil elements inapplicable? If they’re inapplicable, what connects the deceit to the ‘in connection with’ requirement for the purchase or sale?

questions.title: How does the panel justify using an intervening Supreme Court case (Kousisis) that post-dated the district court’s ruling?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed before Kousisis, but the Fifth Circuit applies Kousisis on appeal. Is this simply the normal rule that intervening Supreme Court decisions apply to cases on direct review? Are there any retroactivity or fair-notice concerns given the criminal context?

questions.title: What is the constitutional dimension, if any, to the court’s insistence on money-or-property (post-Ciminelli) as the fraud object?
questions.question_body: Ciminelli grounds its rejection of the right-to-control theory in the federal fraud statutes’ protection of ‘traditional property interests.’ Is the Fifth Circuit’s analysis here purely statutory, or is there a constitutional avoidance or due process vagueness concern pushing courts to confine fraud to traditional property?

questions.title: Why didn’t the panel address potential First Amendment defenses given that the alleged misstatements were social-media posts?
questions.question_body: The conduct involves public statements about securities. Are fraudulent misrepresentations categorically unprotected so the First Amendment plays no role, or did the panel avoid that issue because a Rule 12 indictment challenge isn’t the right vehicle? At what stage would courts evaluate First Amendment arguments in a § 1348 prosecution?

questions.title: What level of specificity must an indictment include to satisfy the double jeopardy notice function in a complex fraud scheme?
questions.question_body: The panel recites that an indictment must ‘provide the defendant with a double jeopardy defense against future prosecutions.’ For a multi-month ‘pump and dump’ scheme with many posts and trades, what factual particulars (timeframe, securities, statements, co-conspirators) are necessary so that a future prosecution would be barred?

questions.title: How does conspiracy under § 1349 interact with the substantive § 1348 offense when the government proceeds on a fraudulent-inducement theory?
questions.question_body: The indictment charges both § 1349 conspiracy and § 1348 substantive counts. If the fraudulent-inducement theory sets the property/intent contours for § 1348, do those same contours (no net-loss requirement; object to obtain money/property) define the conspiracy’s ‘unlawful objective’? Is proof of actual victim loss or reliance still irrelevant for § 1349?

questions.title: What makes the alleged conduct satisfy the ‘in connection with the purchase or sale’ language of § 1348(2)?
questions.question_body: The alleged misstatements were social-media posts about securities and the defendants’ positions. How close must the nexus be between the deceptive statements and the victims’ purchases to meet ‘in connection with’ under § 1348? Is the standard analogous to § 10(b), or is it broader/narrower in criminal prosecutions?

questions.title: Why was aiding-and-abetting liability under 18 U.S.C. § 2 charged alongside primary § 1348 violations?
questions.question_body: The indictment cites § 2. In coordinated ‘pump and dump’ schemes with multiple speakers and traders, what does the government gain by charging aiding and abetting in addition to principal liability, and does it change the required proof for participants who didn’t personally make the misstatements?

questions.title: Must the government identify specific victims or trades in the indictment to allege a ‘scheme to defraud’ of money or property?
questions.question_body: The opinion treats ‘followers’ or ‘other investors’ as the victims induced to purchase. Is it sufficient at the indictment stage to allege a class of victims and a general time period, or must the indictment name specific purchasers, dates, and transactions to show the object was to obtain particular victims’ money or property?
